strengths: Synth-SBDH addresses a relevant clinical NLP resource gap: access to annotated clinical text is restricted, and existing datasets cover limited SBDH categories. Its 8,767 synthetic examples include spans, status, temporality, and rationales across 15 categories.

The downstream experiments establish practical utility, particularly for small-model classification. On MIMIC-SBDH aligned, prompt-based RoBERTa improves from 55.64 to 91.11 macro-F. Evaluation spans two clinical sources, multiple architectures, classification and span extraction, with three-run results and useful analyses of rare categories and training-set size.

Human review is substantial: two experienced annotators assess the entire 1,755-example synthetic test split, adjudicate disagreements, and correct missing and erroneous annotations. The detailed error analysis, including 581 added annotations, provides valuable transparency about synthetic-label limitations.

The generation workflow is understandable, and the appendices document seed examples, prompts, category definitions, annotation guidelines, and training configurations. The reported release of data and checkpoints supports reuse. These materials and the demonstrated classification benefits support a contribution suitable for Findings.
weaknesses: The improvements are less general than the abstract's 'consistently outperform' wording suggests. Encoder NER gains are negligible, and several Mamba and Llama settings show no benefit or regressions. The headline 94.44-point housing improvement involves only 18 positive test examples. T5's large NER gain also starts from an unstable baseline, with macro-F 25.44 ± 18.24. Specify the statistical test and sampling unit behind the p-values, and distinguish training stability from test-sample uncertainty.

The evaluation only partially validates the dataset's advertised coverage. Downstream tasks merge categories, retain positive annotations, and do not evaluate temporal prediction; negative annotations are sparse in Table 10. Synthetic examples average 13.7 words, substantially shorter than both clinical datasets. Moreover, public real-data evaluation covers only four aligned categories, while real-data NER uses private VA data. These facts limit conclusions about comprehensive clinical extraction and independent reproduction of the full evaluation.

The reasoning-distillation claim exceeds the evidence. Table 5 shows only 0.66 and 0.58 absolute macro-F gains, with the latter nonsignificant, on synthetic text from the same generation process. This supports a modest auxiliary-supervision effect, but does not establish transferred reasoning capability or improved rationale faithfulness. Evaluating span predictions on real clinical text would not require gold rationales at test time.

The annotation-quality figures require careful interpretation. The 71.06% human–LLM figure includes newly added annotations in its denominator, whereas GPT-4's 90.78% assessment excludes missing annotations. They therefore measure different things. Experts also review visible GPT-4 annotations, and Appendix E.2 permits retaining any acceptable category for ambiguous spans. A small independently annotated subset and separate category, status, and temporal agreement results would strengthen the benchmark-quality claims.

Some reporting ambiguities obstruct verification. Appendix D.2 describes a matched-step comparison against MIMIC pretraining, but Table 13 does not distinguish that condition from the baseline used in D.1, leaving the claimed synthetic-versus-real comparison unclear. The deduplication rule also specifies similarity above 0.7 with 'all' previous examples, which differs materially from filtering against any matching example. Clarifying these details and comparing against class-balancing baselines would better establish the dataset's added value.
